subject: child-health
title: Newborn care and resuscitation: high-yield essentials for exams

steps.tx: Most newborns breathe and cry within seconds of birth. Resuscitation begins with **drying**, warming, stimulation and positioning, then assessment of breathing, heart rate and colour. A baby who is apnoeic, gasping or has a **heart rate below 100 per minute** needs **positive pressure ventilation** (PPV) as the key intervention, because hypoxia is the usual cause of failure to breathe at birth.

steps.tx: Reassess at each stage by asking three questions: is the baby **breathing**, what is the **heart rate**, and what is the colour? If the heart rate is below 100 per minute or breathing stays inadequate after initial steps, begin **positive pressure ventilation** and confirm the chest rises with each breath. If the heart rate remains below 60 per minute after 30 seconds of effective ventilation, add **chest compressions** coordinated with breaths, using 100% oxygen.

steps.tx: Hypoglycaemia is common after birth, especially in babies of **diabetic mothers** and small or large for dates infants. Maternal hyperglycaemia causes fetal hyperinsulinaemia, which persists after cord clamping. Symptomatic babies, with jitteriness, floppiness or poor feeding, and those with low glucose despite feeding need prompt **intravenous dextrose**, as neurological injury can follow.

steps.tx: Developmental dysplasia of the **hip** is linked to breech presentation and female sex. A click with asymmetric thigh folds suggests instability. In infants under about four to six months, **ultrasound** is preferred because the cartilaginous acetabulum is not seen on X-ray. Clicks alone are not always pathological, so examination should be repeated and referral made when signs are persistent.

steps.tx: Developmental dysplasia of the **hip** is likelier after **breech presentation**, especially in girls. A click with asymmetric thigh folds suggests instability, though clicks alone are not always pathological. In young infants **ultrasound** is preferred because the cartilaginous socket stays invisible on plain film, as this view of the femoral head against the shallow bony roof shows. Repeat the examination and refer when signs persist.
steps.say: This hip ultrasound shows the femoral head seated against a shallow bony roof, which is why early scans matter. Breech birth and female sex raise the risk of hip dysplasia, and a click with uneven thigh folds suggests instability. Ultrasound suits young infants since cartilage stays invisible on plain film. Repeat the exam and refer if signs persist.

steps.tx: Vitamin K deficiency bleeding results from low stores at birth. Routine **prophylaxis** is offered to all newborns, usually as an intramuscular dose soon after birth. If parents decline, discuss the risks clearly, including late bleeding in breastfed babies, and document informed refusal. Coercion is not appropriate, and the baby should be offered oral alternatives where available.
